newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: GM DENIES RECALL WILL AFFECT 300,000 COMMODORES
General Motors Holdens says its recall of late model Commodores does not involve nearly 300-thousand vehicles as suggested in newspaper reports this morning.
The carmaker says it is recalling 120-thousand VR and VS model Commodores fitted with towbars, due to the potential for problems with their automatic transmissions, as announced last week.
And a GMH representative says the company has offered to repair cars that currently don't have towbars, as a precaution in case a future owner fits a towbar.
He says those cars will be fixed next year, after the others have been dealt with.
CHALLENGE TO NSW GUN LAWS
A group planning to challenge the New South Wales gun laws in the Supreme Court, claims the state government is acting illegally in promoting them.
The Hunter Valley Concerned Citizens Assocation has voted to spend about 10-thousand dollars in challenging the laws.
Spokesman, Tony Pitt, says the challenge is being mounted because the gun laws haven't been gazetted, don't have royal assent and, as a result, the government is acting illegally.
He says the Government's advertisements for the laws are just a bluff, and will remain a bluff until the laws are given the royal assent and gazetted.
OPTUS SHARE FLOAT WON'T HAPPEN BEFORE END OF YEAR
One of the key stakeholders in Optus Communications says the sharemarket float of Australia's second telecommunications carrier won't proceed before the end of the year.
Mayne Nickless had been hoping a legal wrangle between shareholders in pay-TV operator, Optus Vision, could be resolved in time for a float this year of the parent company.
Mayne Nickless is selling its entire 25-percent Optus holding in the float, which it now says it's committed to achieving as soon as possible.
BEAZLEY SAYS GOVT SHOULD RUN FULL TERM
Federal Opposition Leader, Kim Beazley, says he finds it hard to believe the Treasurer is on his own in Coalition ranks when he threatens moves that could trigger an early election.
Peter Costello is threatening to return to the Senate rejected legislation that seeks to limit new migrants' access to welfare entitlements.
Senate defeat again would provide the constitutional trigger for an early election.
But Mr Beazley says the Government should run its full term.
He says there's mish-mash in Government thinking on an early election and he suggests there's been a nod and a wink between Mr Costello and the Prime Minister on the issue.
Mr Howard has attempted to downplay Mr Costello's remarks.
SALMONELLA OUTBREAK IN MELBOURNE
Health inspectors are focusing on a Melbourne sandwich bar suspected to be the source of a salmonella outbreak which has left at least 24 people with food poisoning.
The sandwich bar in an eastern suburbs shopping centre has been closed as authorities take samples and interview staff.
It's believed the salmonella is a rare strain, possibly passed on by faeces or contaminated utensils.
Officials say they haven't heard of anyone being admitted to hospital, but a caller has told the ABC her relative has been in hospital for three days.
CREDIT UNIONS HAPPY WITH WALLIS INQUIRY
Credit unions are happy with a discussion paper put out by the Wallis Inquiry into Australia's financial system, saying it identifies the major issues to be addressed.
And Graham Loughlin of the Credit Union Services Corporation says he'd expect a 400-page document to cover the ground.
The Federal Treasurer has called for an assessment of financial deregulation since the early 1980's and recommendations on how to regulate the system in the future.
Mr Loughlin says the discussion paper, released yesterday by inquiry chairman Stan Wallis, identifies all the major issues that have come through in more than 200 submissions.
These include competition, efficiency, and security for consumers as technology advances.
NEW FIGURES ON HIV/AIDS
As red ribbons go on sale in the lead-up to World AIDS day on Sunday, new figures show there are now about 13-thousand people in Australia and New Zealand living with HIV/AIDS.
A United Nations report shows that worldwide 22-and-a-half million people are living with HIV/AIDS, after more than three million new infections this year.
Most of the two-point-seven million newly infected adults, were under 25-years, and nearly half were women.

There were also 400-thousand new infections among children. The report also found the number of HIV infections have exploded in previously little affected parts of Asia, eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union.
APPEAL AGAINST LIFE SENTENCE FOR HIRING WIFE-KILLER
A Sydney businessman, convicted of hiring two men to murder his wife, is asking for a re-determination of his life sentence in the Supreme Court.
Andrew Peter Kalajzich was sentenced to life in prison for the murder of his wife Megan at the couple's home at Fairlight in January, 1986.
He was also sentenced to 14-years jail for conspiracy to murder his wife and 12-years for attempting to discharge a loaded gun with intent to murder.
Kalajzich is asking the Supreme Court to determine a minimum and additional terms to replace his life sentence, under "Truth in Sentencing" legislation.
BLACKHAWK INQUIRY WRAPPING UP EVIDENCE
The Blackhawk inquiry is finishing hearing evidence about the June accident, with some of the issues raised to be passed to the Defence Force for further investigation.
The Military Board of Inquiry has spent 43 days hearing evidence relating to the mid-air collision of two Army Blackhawk helicopters near Townsville.
Eighteen servicemen on a night-time counter terrorism exercise died.
The board was told a range of issues raised during the inquiry were not causes of the accident but may require further investigation.
They relate to a non-standard bolt being fitted to one of the Blackhawk helicopters involved in the crash, the non reporting of some safety incidents and daytime live firing exercises.
